title: Nucleus Decomposition Revisited: An Efficient Counting-Based Approach

statements.text: 1 (𝑘-Clique). A 𝑘-clique is a vertex set 𝐶 ⊆ 𝑉 with |𝐶 | = 𝑘 such that (𝑢, 𝑣) ∈ 𝐸 for every 𝑢, 𝑣 ∈ 𝐶.

1 (Clique Path). In a Succinct Clique Tree, a clique path P is any root-to-leaf path. All clique paths are enumerated in left-to-right depth-first order, with the 𝑖-th path denoted by P𝑖 . Formally, P𝑖 = ⟨𝑣 𝑎1 , 𝑣 𝑎2 , . . . , 𝑣 𝑎ℓ ⟩, where 𝑣 𝑎1 is the root, 𝑣 𝑎ℓ is the leaf, and ℓ is the path length. Example 3.1. Figure 3 shows an example of a SCT. 1 (Unique Path Encoding [19]). For any 𝑘-clique 𝐶𝑘 in the graph, there exists only one clique path P = 𝑉ℎ (P) ∪ 𝑉𝑝 (P) such that 𝑉ℎ (P) ⊆ 𝐶𝑘 ⊆ (𝑉ℎ (P) ∪ 𝑉𝑝 (P)). Here, 𝑉ℎ (P) and 𝑉𝑝 (P) denote the sets of hold vertices and pivot vertices on the path P, respectively. Intuitively, any 𝑘-clique represented by a path P must include all hold vertices of that path, while the pivot vertices are optional. Formally, a 𝑘-clique 𝐶𝑘 is encoded by a CPI path P if and only if 𝑉ℎ (P) ⊆ 𝐶𝑘 ⊆ 𝑉ℎ (P) ∪ 𝑉𝑝 (P); it is covered by P if and only if 𝐶𝑘 ⊆ 𝑉ℎ (P) ∪ 𝑉𝑝 (P). Example 3.2. For SCT as shown in Figure 3. Given an ordered set 𝑉𝑝𝐶 = {𝑣 0, . . . , 𝑣𝑡 −1 }, the updated path set P ′ is defined as:   P ′ = (𝑉𝑝P \ {𝑣 0, . . . , 𝑣𝑖 }, 𝑉ℎP ∪ {𝑣 0, . . . , 𝑣𝑖 −1 }) 𝑖 = 0, . . . , 𝑡 − 1 .

1 (𝑠-Connectivity). Given integers 0 < 𝑟 < 𝑠, two 𝑟 -cliques 𝑅 and 𝑅 ′ in a graph (or subgraph) 𝐻 are said to be 𝑠-connected if there exists a sequence of 𝑟 -cliques 𝑅 = 𝑅1, 𝑅2, . . . , 𝑅𝑡 = 𝑅 ′, referred to as an 𝑠-clique path, such that for each 𝑖 ∈ {1, . . . , 𝑡 − 1} there exists an induced 𝑠-clique 𝑆𝑖 ⊆ 𝑉 (𝐻 ) satisfying 𝑅𝑖 ∪ 𝑅𝑖+1 ⊆ 𝑆𝑖 .
1 (Clique Connectivity). Given Two 𝑟 -cliques 𝐶 and 𝐶 ′ and a clique path P of the CPI, if 𝐶 ⊆ P and 𝐶 ′ ⊆ P, then 𝐶 and 𝐶 ′ are 𝑠-connected.

proofs.text: Every 𝑠-clique on the path is 𝑉ℎ ∪ 𝑄 with 𝑄 ⊆ 𝑉𝑝 and |𝑄 | = 𝑠 − ℎ (Lemma 3.1). Fix any 𝑟 -clique 𝐶𝑟 and let 𝑏 = |𝐶𝑟 ∩ 𝑉𝑝 |. Since 𝐶𝑟 already contributes those 𝑏 pivots, an 𝑠-clique containing 𝐶𝑟 is obtained precisely by choosing the remaining 𝑠 − ℎ − 𝑏 pivots from the 𝑝 − 𝑏 unused pivots in 𝑉𝑝 . The number of such −𝑏  choices is 𝑠 𝑝−ℎ−𝑏 , which is zero whenever the lower or upper bound is violated. □

(⇒)According to Lemma 3.1, all 𝑠-cliques on P consist of vertices from 𝑉ℎ (P) and 𝑉𝑝 (P). Therefore, if 𝑠 < |𝑉ℎ (P)|, it is impossible for any 𝑠-clique to include all hold vertices, and thus no 𝑠-clique exists. Similarly, if 𝑠 > |𝑉ℎ (P)| + |𝑉𝑝 (P)|, it is impossible for any 𝑠-clique to include all hold vertices and enough pivot vertices, and thus no 𝑠-clique exists. (⇐)Conversely, if 𝑠 lies within this interval, we can construct at least one 𝑠-clique based on Lemma 3.1, ensuring the existence of at least one 𝑠-clique. □

Let P be a path in the CPI B. By Lemma 3.3, if P survives the pruning rule, it contains at least one 𝑠-clique. Thus, every path in P𝑠 contains at least one 𝑠-clique. Therefore, the number of 𝑠-cliques is greater than or equal to the number of CPI paths in P𝑠 . By definition of P𝑠 , each 𝑃 ∈ P𝑠 satisfies |𝑉ℎ (𝑃)| ≤ 𝑠. Thus Í □

On a CPI path, holds are mandatory and pivots optional. For each 𝑖, promoting 𝑣 0, . . . , 𝑣𝑖 −1 to holds and deleting 𝑣𝑖 keeps the path valid and forbids any clique that contains all pivots of 𝐶, so no subpath encodes 𝐶 (soundness). For any surviving clique 𝐾, let 𝑖 be the first index with 𝑣𝑖 ∉ 𝐾; then 𝐾 contains the promoted prefix and excludes 𝑣𝑖 , hence is encoded precisely on subpath 𝑖 and on no other (completeness & uniqueness). □

We prove the theorem separately for three distinct cases. (1) If 𝑒 is a hold-hold edge, every encoded clique would require both endpoints, which becomes impossible after deleting 𝑒; hence, the path is invalid. (2) If 𝑒 is a hold-pivot edge, all encoded cliques must retain the hold endpoint. Thus, we update the path with respect to the pivot endpoint. By Lemma 3.1, every 𝑘-clique encoded by a path P must contain all hold vertices on that path, whereas pivot vertices are optional. If the removed vertex 𝑣 lies in the hold set 𝑉ℎ (P), no encoded 𝑘-clique can survive, so the whole path vanishes. If 𝑣 ∈ 𝑉𝑝 (P), only those cliques that actually include 𝑣 disappear; the cliques formed by the unchanged hold set and the remaining pivots are still uniquely represented by the shortened path, so we remove 𝑣 and keep the rest of P intact. □

If 𝐶 ⊆ P and 𝐶 ′ ⊆ P, then there exists a sequence of 𝑟 -cliques 𝐶 = 𝐶 1, 𝐶 2, . . . , 𝐶 𝑘 = 𝐶 ′ such that each consecutive pair 𝐶 𝑖 and 𝐶 𝑖+1 are 𝑠-connected. This is because each 𝑟 -clique in the sequence shares an 𝑠-clique with the next one, as they are all part of the same clique path P. Therefore, by the definition of 𝑠-connectedness, 𝐶 and 𝐶 ′ are 𝑠-connected. □
